title: Sabha: Indraprastha
hook: a message from a dead father: Pandu, through Narada, asks his son to perform the Rajasuya

segments.voice: Yesterday, the halls of the gods, as Narada described them in Yudhishthira's sabha: each one known by who sits there — here is what the sky looks like. Did you widen the frame on something? Day seven hundred fifty.

Yudhishthira has been listening closely. And he's noticed something. In the hall of Indra, among all the sages and gods, Narada named only one human king: Harishchandra. Not the great kings of Yudhishthira's own line, not the heroes of the old stories. One name. Why him? the king asks. What did he do? And there's a second question, the one underneath. In the hall of Yama, among the dead, you saw my father. You saw Pandu. What did he say?
screen: `ONE KING IN INDRA'S HALL.` → `WHY HARISHCHANDRA?` → `AND MY FATHER?`

segments.voice: Narada answers the first question first. Harishchandra, he says, was a mighty king who brought other kings under him and then performed the great sacrifice called the Rajasuya. He gave generously to everyone who came. And because of that sacrifice, he shines in Indra's hall. Then the second answer. Narada had seen Pandu in Yama's hall, and Pandu had seen Harishchandra's place. So Pandu gave Narada a message to carry. Tell my son, Pandu said: you are able to conquer the earth, and your brothers obey you. Perform the Rajasuya. Then I, and our ancestors, may go to Indra's world. Sit with that for a moment. Yudhishthira's father died when the brothers were young, back in the forest. He has been gone for this whole long serial. And now, in the brand-new hall, in front of everyone, a sage turns and delivers his words. Not comfort. Not, I'm proud of you. A request, and a heavy one. There's something tender in it, though. Pandu is still thinking of his sons, and still thinking of his own fathers before him. The message runs both ways down the line. A son is asked to do something for a father, so that the father can rise with his ancestors. And notice how it reaches him: not as a dream, not as a ghost, but through a guest in the sabha. The hall that was opened by feeding people is now the place where the dead can speak to the living. Tomorrow, Narada adds something to the message that isn't nearly as welcome.
screen: `HARISHCHANDRA'S SACRIFICE.` · `PANDU SAW IT FROM YAMA'S HALL.` · `TELL MY SON: PERFORM THE RAJASUYA.` · `A FATHER, A SON, THE ANCESTORS.` · then, large: `THE DEAD SPEAK IN THE SABHA.`

segments.voice: Go gently with this one. Settle the breath. Bring to mind a parent, a grandparent, or an elder, living or gone, and something they hoped for you. It might be large or small, spoken or never quite said. You don't need to agree with it, or act on it. Just let it be heard, the way Yudhishthira hears his father's words. If you pray, you can hold that person in mind as you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Sabha. A hall, and its assembly. Today, in Yudhishthira's sabha, a sage carries a message from his father among the dead.
Your line: tell my son. Today, pass on a kind word someone said about another person, to the person it was about. Day seven hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Hindu families honor their ancestors in shraddha rites, with offerings of food and water, and in the season of Pitru Paksha, when the ancestors are remembered together.

fork.setup: you're Yudhishthira. Narada has named one human king in Indra's hall. what do you ask him?
options: why that king, and what my father said.
whether your own hall will be remembered.
fork.reveal: he asks about Harishchandra and then about Pandu, and learns his father's request: perform the Rajasuya.

original.note: Sanskrit hariścandra: the king Narada names in Indra's hall, there because of his Rajasuya.

trapdoor: what you thought: a ghost story.
what it means: a father's request, carried by a sage, that his son perform the Rajasuya.
what a scholar hears: Pandu's request is for himself and the ancestors too, binding a son's deed to his whole line.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Lokapala Sabhakhyana Parva (Yudhishthira asks about Harishchandra and Pandu; Narada delivers Pandu's message)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm that Narada names Harishchandra as the human king in Indra's hall and attributes his place to the Rajasuya and his generosity.
Confirm wording of Pandu's message: Yudhishthira able to subjugate the earth, brothers obedient, perform the Rajasuya so that Pandu and the ancestors may go to Indra's world.
'Died when the brothers were young, back in the forest' refers to Adi Parva; confirm phrasing.
howItsDone: confirm shraddha and Pitru Paksha description.
